title: Compute-Matched Evaluation Reveals Task-Dependent Diffusion Planning Advantage

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable a fair comparison between diffusion and autoregressive language models by isolating the generation paradigm from inference budget. Paper [12] explicitly conducts a controlled comparison between autoregressive and masked diffusion language models, isolating the generation paradigm as the sole variable. This matches the purpose at the problem-class level, as both contributions aim to compare these paradigms under controlled conditions. Paper [3] also compares generation quality and diversity between discrete diffusion and autoregressive models, but its focus is on generation quality/diversity rather than isolating inference budget effects, so it does not fully match the purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves a compute-matched evaluation protocol that calibrates autoregressive best-of-k sampling such that `k*t_AR` matches the diffusion model's wall-clock time per instance, using a held-out calibration set. Paper [8] discusses best-of-k sampling in the context of inference-time alignment but does not match the specific compute-matching protocol described here. Paper [12] uses identical compute budgets for both paradigms (autoregressive and masked diffusion) to isolate the generation paradigm, which is substantively equivalent to the compute-matching mechanism described in this contribution. Paper [28] and [25] explore inference-time compute scaling but do not involve compute-matching protocols for autoregressive best-of-k sampling.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves timing measurements on A100-80GB hardware, robustness checks with median vs p75 timing estimators, and application to specific tasks (Countdown and Mini Sudoku). Paper [12] uses identical hardware (NVIDIA H100 80GB) and identical compute budgets for both paradigms, isolating the generation paradigm as the sole variable, which matches the evaluation design at the benchmark family level. Paper [8] and [25] also explore inference-time compute scaling but do not use the same evaluation design (timing estimators or task-specific robustness checks). No prior paper introduces a genuinely new evaluation design matching this contribution's specifics.

### Domain
The domain is evaluation methodology for planning/reasoning language models, specifically comparing diffusion and autoregressive paradigms. Paper [12] operates in the same general application area of comparing autoregressive and diffusion-based language models, which covers the domain facet. Paper [3] also compares these paradigms but focuses on generation quality/diversity rather than planning/reasoning tasks, so it does not match the domain as closely. Papers [9] and [4] address reasoning tasks but do not focus on evaluation methodology for comparing diffusion vs autoregressive models.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to determine whether diffusion's reported planning advantage survives compute matching. This specific empirical relationship — comparing planning performance between diffusion and autoregressive models under compute-matched conditions — is not established in any prior paper. While several papers (e.g., [1], [3], [5]) discuss diffusion's planning advantages, none explicitly investigate compute-matched comparisons or survival of the advantage under such conditions. Therefore, no prior paper reports the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves evaluating Dream-7B (diffusion) against its autoregressive initializer Qwen2.5-7B under greedy, compute-matched best-of-k, and diffusion conditions on two Reasoning Gym tasks (Countdown, Mini Sudoku). Papers [1], [3], and [5] describe diffusion models and their planning capabilities, but none use the specific experimental setup of compute-matched comparisons across greedy, best-of-k, and diffusion sampling strategies. While [5] explores diffusion vs. autoregressive models in data-constrained settings, it does not employ the same mechanism or experimental design. Thus, the mechanism is uncovered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves task-dependent results comparing performance on Countdown and Mini Sudoku under compute-matched conditions. Papers [8], [13], [14], [16], and [17] discuss self-consistency and adaptive sampling techniques for reasoning tasks, but none use compute-matched comparisons or the specific Reasoning Gym tasks. While [18] introduces functional benchmarks for reasoning evaluation, it does not employ compute-matched comparisons or the same statistical framework. No prior paper uses this evaluation design, making it uncovered.

### Domain
The domain is planning tasks, specifically sequential arithmetic (Countdown) and constraint satisfaction (Mini Sudoku). Papers [1], [3], [5], and [10] address planning tasks broadly, including reasoning and constraint satisfaction. While the specific tasks (Countdown and Mini Sudoku) are new instances, the general application area of planning tasks is covered by prior work. Therefore, the domain is covered.
